t: the order of inheritances. The order of priority in inheritance.
and males precede females. Sons precede daughters.

in every place a female has no inheritance with a male. At every stage of priority in inheritance, if there is a male and a female of the same degree of family relationship, the males inherit and not the females (but if the female is of a closer degree of relationship she precedes the male).

and this matter is from tradition. In the tradition of the Oral Torah. For the Torah has no explicit reference to inheritance by parents, and the Sages found in the text an allusion that a father inherits his son (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 8:1).
those who come out of his loins. His offspring.
no son of his is found in the world. The son died.
we examine the offspring of the son. We check whether his son has any descendants at all, even after many generations.

the offspring of the father who are the brothers of the deceased. The deceased's brothers on his father's side (for relatives on the mother's side are not considered family for inheritance, as below, halacha 6).
offspring of brothers. Descendants of his brother or sister.
the inheritance moves and goes up to Reuven. We check in the generations before the deceased whether he has relatives, even up to Reuven son of our father Jacob.
to the head of the generations. The earlier generations.

there is no Israelite who has no heir. Unlike a convert, whose family lineage was cancelled after he converted (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 14:11), and if he dies without children he has no heirs and whoever is first to take possession of his property acquires it (Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 1:6).
she precedes. Because she is of the offspring of the son, who precedes the daughter, and all who come out of the loins of one who precedes in inheritance precede (above, halacha 3).
the grandfather. The patriarch.

the three sons of his son inherit half the estate and the daughter of his son inherits the half. The three sons of his son inherit half by virtue of their father, and the daughter of the other son inherits half by virtue of her father.

the mother's family is not called a family. And likewise regarding levirate marriage and chalitzah (see Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 1:7). And with regard to testimony and mourning, relatives of the mother's family are considered relatives by rabbinic law (see Hilchot Edut 13:1, Hilchot Evel 2:1).
and whether his brother is from his father only or his brother is from his father and his mother. In both cases their law is the same.
all relatives through a transgression. Who were born from a forbidden union.
mamzer. Born from forbidden sexual relations (except one born of a menstruating woman, Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 15:1).
the maidservant. A Canaanite maidservant, who is forbidden to an Israelite.

is not a son. He is not considered his son and is a gentile or slave like his mother (see there, halacha 4, Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 1:4), and even when he converts or is freed he does not inherit his father.
by rabbinic law. By rabbinic enactment.
and he precedes everyone in inheriting her. Even her children (see also Hilchot Ishut 22:1).

even though she is forbidden to him. By a negative or positive commandment, but he has kiddushin with her (there 22:4). But if she is forbidden by a forbidden sexual relation, kiddushin does not take effect with her and he does not inherit her (there 4:12).
a widow to a High Priest. Who is forbidden to him by a negative commandment (there 1:7, Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 17:1).
a divorcee. Who is forbidden to kohanim by a negative commandment (there).

and a chalutzah. A woman whose husband died without children and who performed chalitzah with his brother (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 1:1-2). The law of a chalutzah is like a divorcee, and she is forbidden to a kohen by rabbinic law (Hilchot Ishut 1:7, Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 17:7).
even if she is a minor and even if the husband is a deaf-mute. Whose kiddushin is valid only by rabbinic law (Hilchot Ishut 4:8-9; for the definition of a minor girl see there 2:1-3).
we have already explained in Hilchot Ishut. 22:1-4.
until she enters his domain. Until she leaves her father's domain and enters her husband's domain, but before that he does not inherit her, even after the betrothal (see there).

and a hearing man does not inherit a deaf woman. Who neither hears nor speaks (there 2:26), for she is considered one who lacks understanding, and when she married she did not acquire property for him so that he might inherit her (see there 22:4).
and there we explained. Hilchot Ishut 22:7.

all the property of his wife that came into her possession and was held. The husband inherits only property that was in his wife's possession at the time she died. But property that came into her possession after her death, he does not inherit, as below, halacha 11.

whether property that she brought him as her dowry or property that she did not bring him. Whether she brought it into his possession and it was written in the ketubah document when they married, or she kept the property for herself (see Hilchot Ishut 16:1-2).
doubtful divorce. For example, see Hilchot Gerushin 1:21.

a minor girl who does not need mi'un (refusal). A minor girl whose father died and whom her mother or brothers married off, her kiddushin takes effect by rabbinic law. And if she refuses and says she does not want this husband, she leaves without a get (see Hilchot Ishut 4:8, Hilchot Gerushin 11:8-11). A girl younger than six, or between six and ten who does not know how to safeguard her kiddushin and does not understand their importance, is not betrothed at all and does not even need mi'un (Hilchot Ishut 4:7, Hilchot Gerushin 11:7).
for the Sages did not institute marriage for them. See also Hilchot Ishut 4:9.
her offspring. For example, her son from another husband.
property that is due to come afterward. For the definition and details of property that is due and property that is held, see below 3:1-5.

and likewise a husband does not inherit his wife while in the grave. Unlike other heirs, who inherit by virtue of family relationship (blood relation), so that if they die the right of inheritance passes to their heirs (as above, halacha 3), the husband inherits his wife by virtue of the marriage, so that with his death his right lapses, and he does not bequeath it to his relatives.
one who died and afterward his mother died. And he has a brother from his father but not from his mother (and this refers to a case where his father died and does not inherit his wife).

we do not say: since had the son been alive he would have preceded. We do not say that the dead son inherits his mother and from him the inheritance passes to his brother, who is his relative on his father's side and fit to inherit him. And although in other cases inheritance takes effect through a blood relationship even in the grave (for example, a son who inherits his mother's father even after his mother has died), here it is different because this is a transfer of an estate from one family to another. And in this respect the inheritance of a mother is like the inheritance of a husband (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 159b).

even if he was a day-old infant whose months were not completed. Who was born before nine months had passed from the day his mother conceived. And although for various matters in halacha he is considered a nefel (non-viable birth; see Hilchot Evel 1:6-7), with regard to inheritance he inherits and bequeaths, since he lived for an hour and in that hour he inherited.
the firstborn takes a double portion. Double the portion that each of the other brothers receives in the inheritance.
the ordinary sons. The sons who are not the firstborn.
a sixth. A sixth.
a fifth. A fifth.
a tenth. A tenth.

a firstborn who was born after his father's death. And another brother was born after him (for example, if his mother bore twins and the father died before the first was born, or if sons were born to his father from another wife).

'But he shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the unloved wife'. The continuation of the verse: 'by giving him a double portion,' and from here it follows that only when the father acknowledged the firstborn in his lifetime does he take a double portion.
and if his forehead emerged, etc.. The forehead; with the emergence of the forehead the fetus is considered born (similarly see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 10:6, Hilchot Bikkurim 11:15).
a firstborn who was torn. Where it was not known whether he is male or female (a tumtum), and the membrane covering his sexual organs was torn.

does not diminish. He is not counted in calculating the firstborn's portion (but after the firstborn receives his portion, the ordinary son who was torn divides equally with the other brothers, as explained shortly).

the firstborn takes a quarter of the estate as the firstborn's portion, etc.. With regard to the firstborn's portion the tumtum is not counted, and therefore the firstborn takes a quarter of the property. [In another version: 'The firstborn takes half the estate, as if there were with him only the two ordinary sons, and the remaining half is divided equally by the two ordinary sons with the one who was torn.' According to this version (which is apparently from the first edition), the firstborn first takes his entire share of the inheritance and afterward his brothers divide the rest.]

a one-day-old infant diminishes the firstborn's portion, etc.. If he was born before his father died he is counted as an heir in calculating the firstborn's portion, but not a fetus that died. And likewise one born after his father's death is not counted in calculating the firstborn's portion, though he receives a share of the inheritance (see Rabbeinu Yosef Migash, Bava Batra 142b).
for example, one who was mixed up with another. And it is not clear which of the brothers is the firstborn.
and how do they proceed?. If they want to take the firstborn's portion.
if they were recognized and afterward mixed up. That at first it was known who the firstborn was and afterward they got mixed up, so that one of them has the right to take the firstborn's portion.
power of attorney. Authorization, whereby one appoints the other as his agent to take the firstborn's portion from their brothers and they divide it between themselves.
who were born in one hiding place. In one place of concealment, and already at the time of birth it was not known who was the firstborn.

we do not write a power of attorney, and there is no firstborn's portion here. The Sages learned from the verses that only a firstborn who was recognized as definitely the firstborn at birth receives a firstborn's portion (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 127a), and since no firstborn was recognized, writing a power of attorney is of no help.
the grandfather. The patriarch.
the son of the ordinary son inherits in the grandfather's estate a third, etc.. For descendants stand in place of their fathers and inherit their share in the grandfather's property (as above 1:5).

and the same law applies to the sons of brothers and the sons of the father's brothers and all heirs. In the case where the deceased has no descendants and his other relatives inherit him (as above 1:3). And since these sons inherit by virtue of their father, one whose father was a firstborn takes a double portion over the sons of the other heirs (for example, if one of the brothers died without descendants and his brothers' sons come to inherit him, the sons of the firstborn brother take double compared to the sons of the other brothers).
firstborn for inheritance. Who was born first to his father and inherits a double portion of his property.
peter rechem. Who was born first to his mother, and although he is firstborn to his mother he does not take a double portion in her estate.
his strength. His power, his seed.
one who comes after nefalim. Born after his mother bore a nefel.

even if the head of the nefel emerged alive, etc.. Although at the emergence of the head it was alive and the emergence of the head defines it as born, the one who comes after it is considered the firstborn, for a child born before nine months of pregnancy who dies within thirty days is defined as a nefel (Hilchot Milah 1:13, Commentary on the Mishnah, Niddah 5:3).
a nine-month child. Born after nine months of pregnancy, and defined as viable.
for no child had been born to him before this one who came out alive into the air of the world. And one born before nine months is not defined as living until he lives thirty days.
whose majority of the head emerged alive. For at the emergence of the majority of the head, which counts as birth, he was still alive.
one born by caesarean. A child who did not emerge through the opening of the womb but by cutting the wall of the abdomen (caesarean section).
who was not born. Who was not born in the usual way (and similarly see Hilchot Bikkurim 11:16, Hilchot Bechorot 2:4).
for another preceded him. And only one who is 'the first of his strength' inherits a double portion (above, halacha 9).
in his gentile state. When he was a gentile.

he has no firstborn for inheritance. For the first son born to him when he was a gentile no longer has a family relationship to him, and the son born to him after he converted is not 'the first of his strength.'
since he is not called his son. He is not considered his son at all (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 1:4).

the one who comes after him... a firstborn for inheritance. The son born of an Israelite woman is 'the first of his strength,' and not the one born of the gentile woman, because he is not called his son at all (unlike a gentile who converted, who was considered his son before he converted).
if the firstborn was a mamzer. Born of forbidden sexual relations (and he inherits like a son born legitimately, as above 1:7).
this one who is hated in her marriage. A woman whom it is forbidden to marry.
and needless to say if he was the son of a divorcee or the son of a chalutzah. Whose marriages to kohanim do not carry the penalty of karet and kiddushin takes effect with them.
are believed regarding the firstborn. To testify about the child that he is the firstborn, and he will inherit a double portion.
a midwife immediately. The midwife ('chayah') is believed immediately after the birth to testify about one of the newborns that he emerged first.
and his mother, all seven days of the birth, is believed to say 'this is the firstborn'. Some explain the reason is that during these days he is mainly with his mother (Tosafot Rosh, Kiddushin 74a).
and his father always. Even after his son has grown.

even if the father said, etc.. From the verse 'he shall acknowledge the firstborn' (Deuteronomy 21:17), the Sages expounded that a father is believed to recognize and testify about his son, and this applies both to the firstborn and to other matters of lineage and personal status (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 15:15-16).
the father who became mute. Lost the ability to speak, and it is not known whether he is of sound mind.
we examine him. Whether he gives correct answers to questions by nodding or hinting.

in the way that we examine for gittin. A husband who became mute and wants to divorce his wife; if his mind is deranged he cannot divorce her (for the manner of examination see Hilchot Gerushin 2:16).
he says such and such things, etc.. A certain reference in the course of ordinary conversation, and from these words it appears that this is his firstborn.
until he says, 'This is my firstborn son'. For then it is understood that he means that he is the firstborn of him.
in property that is due to come after his father's death. Property that came into the father's hands after his death and was not actually in his possession at the time of his death.
in property held by his father that came into his possession. Which belonged to the father and was also under his control.

in all that is found with him. The verse says: 'by giving him a double portion of all that he has,' and from here it follows that the law of taking a double portion applies only to property found in the father's possession at the time of his death.
equally. In equal shares.
a loan. A loan that the father made and died before it was repaid.
a ship at sea. And it is in doubt whether it will return. Although the loan and the ship belong to the father, nevertheless they are not actually in his hand.
rented or leased. That their father rented to others for money or produce.
that was grazing in the open country. Grazing areas outside the settlement.
and gave birth. After their father died.

he takes a double portion of it and its offspring. Although the cow was not in the father's hands (but in the hands of others or in an ownerless place), since it is his property it is considered held by him for purposes of the firstborn. And the increase that the animal gained by fattening or giving birth is also considered in the father's possession (and see below, halacha 4).

one of his father's acquaintances slaughtered, etc.. One who slaughters an animal must give the foreleg, jaw and stomach to the kohen (see Hilchot Bikkurim 9:1). Here the father was a kohen, and one of his acquaintances was accustomed to give him those gifts.
he takes a double portion. For these gifts are considered in the father's possession already from the time the animal was slaughtered.
the firstborn does not take a double portion in the increase that the property gained after his father's death. For it was not held by the father at the time of death.

he assesses that increase in money. After the firstborn takes a double portion of the property, he assesses the value of its increase, and the money for the portion that exceeds his share he gives to his brothers so that all take the increase equally.
karmel. Moist, unripened grain.
and kafniyot. Dates while still unripe.
and land that rose with silt. Land onto which alluvium was deposited, and as a result it improved.

but if they improved by themselves and did not change... he takes a double portion in this increase. For whatever grew by itself and did not change is considered the very same thing that the father bequeathed, and the increase is secondary to it.
even though it is by a document. And with a loan by document all the debtor's property is mortgaged to the lender (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 11:4).
and even though the orphans collected land. And we do not say that the land is considered held by their father because it always stays in its place (see there 5:9).
a loan in the firstborn's hand. That the father lent to the firstborn.

a firstborn who sold the firstborn's portion before the division, his sale stands. Although the brothers have not yet divided the property among themselves, the firstborn can sell his firstborn's portion and the sale is valid (and of course he may sell his share as an ordinary son before division, and likewise the brothers their shares; Tosafot, Bava Batra 126b).
for the firstborn has a firstborn's portion before division. From the time the father died, the firstborn's portion is considered his.
therefore, if he divided with his brothers in some of the property. There was property in which he divided equally with his brothers and did not take a double portion.

he waived in all the property. Since the firstborn's portion in all the property is considered his, if he waived it in one place and took as an ordinary son, he revealed that he waives his special portion in all of it.
in what case is this said?. That if he divided equally with his brothers in part of the property, he waived the firstborn's portion.
he did not waive. Because harvesting does not change the grapes in an essential way.
but if they trod them. And it is no longer grapes but wine.
he waived in all the property. Since the grapes changed in an essential way, his protest regarding the grapes is not a protest regarding the wine, and he should have protested anew.
one who performs levirate marriage with his brother's wife. His brother died without children and he married his wife.

he inherits all his brother's held property. Although a father precedes brothers in inheritance and if there is no father the brothers divide the inheritance among themselves, in a case where one of the brothers performs levirate marriage he inherits all of the deceased's property.

for Scripture called him 'the firstborn'. According to the tradition of the Sages, the 'firstborn' in the verse refers not only to the son the yevamah bears to the yavam but also to the brother who performs levirate marriage (compare Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 2:6), who marries the wife of the brother who died, stands in his place and also inherits him. And from the fact that he is called 'firstborn' it is learned that he is considered a firstborn in that his inheritance of his brother is only from the property held in his hands at the time he died.

so he does not take in the increase that property gained after his father's death, etc.. When the father died and before the inheritance was divided the brother died, the yavam receives, in addition to his own share in his father's property, also his brother's share in their father's inheritance. And if this property improved before they divided the inheritance, the yavam does not take in the increase, because it was not held in the hand of the brother who died.

and even if the property improved after he performed levirate marriage and before they divided. Even if the increase came after he performed levirate marriage when he had already in principle acquired his brother's share, since they did not actually divide the inheritance, the increase is not considered held by him.

since the father died in the lifetime of all of them. The yavam receives his brother's share in the father's inheritance as well only in the case where the father died before the brother. But if the brother died and only afterward the father died, the yavam does not receive his brother's share, because at the time the brother died the father's inheritance was not yet held by him and was in the category of 'due,' and so it will be divided among the father's heirs as is the law in general.
in Hilchot Shecheinim. 12:2.
in one boundary. In one place adjacent to each other.
one who awaits a yavam. A woman whose husband died without children and who waits for his brother to marry her.

ma'amar. By Torah law the yavam does not need to betroth his yevamah (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 1:1), but the Sages ruled that he must betroth her before he has relations with her. This kiddushin is called 'ma'amar' and is not complete kiddushin (there 2:1).

the family of her father's house inherits, etc.. A woman awaiting a yavam is in an intermediate state until she is married by levirate marriage, so if she dies her property is divided between her heirs and her husband's heirs, according to the degree of their presumptive ownership of that property.

the family of her father's house inherits melog property. Melog property is property the woman brought into the marriage, which is presumed to be the woman's, and the husband eats its produce (Hilchot Ishut 16:1). And since it was in her possession even while she was married and only the produce was the husband's, the family of her father's house inherits it.

and half of the tzon barzel property. Tzon barzel property is property the woman brought, for which the husband accepted responsibility to return it at the same value he received it (there). The status of this property was not determined as to whether it is presumed to belong to the husband or the wife, and therefore the heirs of the husband and of the wife divide it between them (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yevamot 4:3).
her ketubah. The money the husband obligates himself at the time of the marriage to pay his wife if he divorces her or dies, and it is presumed to belong to the husband.
since they inherited her ketubah. And the Sages ordained that the husband is obligated for her burial in exchange for inheriting her ketubah (Hilchot Ishut 12:4).
as we explained in its place. Hilchot Ishut 22:10.
who are not presumed to be his relatives. Who are not known as his relatives.
he is believed and will inherit him. For he could give them his property as a gift.
a person on his deathbed. A dangerously ill person about to die.
even if he became mute... we examine him as we examine for gittin. See above 2:15 for the explanation.
he is believed about one who is presumed to be his son. Just as he is believed to testify who the firstborn is, as above 2:14.

although he is not believed to say of him 'he is not my son' with regard to lineage. For the father has credibility to testify only about the lineage of his son, and therefore when the son has children the father is no longer believed to testify about his son's lineage, since this has implications also for the son's son (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 15:15).
he is to me like a slave. Who obeys him like a slave in all his needs and requests.
the customs house. Where travelers pay tax on their property, including their slaves.
to smuggle past the customs. So that he will not pay tax on him.
he said at the customs house, 'He is my slave,' and then said, 'He is my son,' he is not believed. For a person does not simply obligate himself at the customs and call his son 'my slave.'
Abba... Imma. A title of respect that was placed before a person's name.
lest a mishap result and this son be impaired. For if the master's son calls the slave and maidservant 'Abba' and 'Imma,' people might think that he is their son and a slave.
and there is a rumor about them. A known and widely spread matter.
maidservant. A gentile maidservant, whose son born from her follows her and is also considered a slave.
the conduct of sons. That he treated him as his son.
and freed. And a freed maidservant has the law of a convert, and her son is an Israelite and follows his father's lineage.

if he is a Torah scholar, etc.. These people know the prohibition against having relations with a maidservant, and it is presumed of them that they would not have relations with her while she was a maidservant but would free her beforehand.

he may not marry an Israelite woman. For lineage purposes the son is considered a slave, and only for inheritance purposes is he considered an Israelite (for the reason for the difference between inheritance and lineage see Maggid Mishneh).
those who make themselves ownerless for this. Who are not careful about the prohibition of relations with a maidservant.
and his brothers from his father may sell him. They may sell him as a slave.
and if his father has no one besides him. Other offspring.
his father's wife is subject to levirate marriage. Like the law of the wife of a man who died and left no descendants, and this son is not considered his offspring (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 1:4).
the fundamentals of the tradition. The principles of the Oral Torah.

and there is one who does not distinguish between the fit and the rest of the people, etc.. Those who hold this opinion maintain that the distinction between one whose father is among the fit and one whose father is among the ordinary people is correct for all laws except for selling him as a slave. For with regard to selling the son as a slave, in any case his brothers cannot sell him.

and there is one who ruled, etc.. According to this view there is no difference at all whether the father is a fit Israelite or an ordinary person, and in any case the son is considered an Israelite (for the reasons for the views see Hilchot Gerushin 10:19).

witnesses who testified that this one is presumed by us to be his son... even though they are not witnesses of lineage and do not know the truth of lineages. That they cannot testify that he is the son of a particular woman who was his father's wife (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 20:5-8), but they testify that it is known and accepted in the community that he is his son.
inherit on the basis of this testimony. And we rely on the presumption even regarding capital matters (there 1:20).
and no son was presumed his except the two of them. No other sons are known.
from the market. From outside.
Shimon takes half the estate. And does not divide the inheritance with Levi, since he does not admit that he is their brother.
a sixth. A sixth. The remaining part after Reuven and Shimon took their shares.
Levi died. And left no children.
the sixth returns to Reuven. For Reuven gave Levi the sixth from his share in the inheritance.
property fell to Levi from others. That he inherited his relatives (for example his wife or his sons who are not his brothers' relatives) or acquired property and the like, and afterward Levi died.
for Reuven admits. And Shimon did not deny it.
the sixth improved by itself. For example, the land that Levi received from Reuven produced fruit and Levi did not spend anything on it.

if it is an increase that reaches the shoulders, etc.. When the fruit is about to be detached and carried on the shoulders, it has the law of detached produce and does not belong to the land, and therefore it is considered separate property and does not return to Reuven with the land, but Reuven and Shimon divide it equally.
and if they had not yet reached harvesting, they belong to Reuven alone. For their law is that of land, and since the land returns to Reuven, the fruit on it returns to him as well.
as we explained. In the first paragraph of the halacha.
Shimon inherits nothing from him. For according to his claim Levi is not his brother.
a doubt has nothing. According to the rule that the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to take from his fellow (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yevamot 11:7).

and a tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered and it is not discernible whether he is male or female (Hilchot Ishut 2:25). [Note: In the Commentary on the Mishnah Maimonides vocalizes this word: tumtom.]
androgynos. One who has male and female sexual organs (there, halacha 24). The halachic status of the tumtum and the androgynos is in doubt whether they have the law of a son or a daughter.
like one of the daughters. The tumtum or androgynos takes a share like one of the daughters, for even if he is not a son, he is entitled at least to the share of one of the daughters.
in Hilchot Ishut. 19:10-20, 20:3-10.
for their maintenance. In the ketubah the husband obligates himself that the daughters will receive maintenance from his property until they come of age or are betrothed (there 19:10).
and for their support. By rabbinic enactment the father must give each of his daughters about a tenth of his property for the needs of her marriage (there 20:1-3).

for maintenance is among the conditions of the ketubah. The obligation of maintenance is among the obligations the Sages imposed on one who is about to marry, and its collection is like collection of the ketubah. By contrast, support is not among the conditions of the ketubah but is defined as a debt, and its method of collection is like that of a debt (see there 20:5-6).
when the estate is large. When the inherited property exceeds what is needed for the maintenance of the sons and daughters until the daughters come of age (there 19:17).
a tenth. A tenth.
everything for the maintenance of the daughters. And the sons will go begging at doors (there).

and they push the tumtum toward the daughters, etc.. Since his status is in doubt, his position is the weaker one: with a large estate he takes like the daughters, and with a small estate he goes begging at doors like the sons. The same applies to an androgynos.

who did not wait three months after her husband. Which is the time a woman who was divorced or widowed must wait before marrying so that it can be recognized whether she is pregnant by her first husband (Hilchot Gerushin 11:18).
a nine-month child to the first. That the fetus was born after nine months of pregnancy and is the son of her first husband.
and if the son died. And the son has no offspring.
both inherit. Both doubtful fathers.

a yevamah who did not wait three months, etc.. A woman whose husband died must wait three months before levirate marriage so that it can be recognized whether she became pregnant by her first husband and does not need levirate marriage (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 1:19). And if she did not wait and gave birth six months after the time of the levirate marriage, the son is possibly a nine-month child of the first husband who died or a seven-month child of the yavam, and the yavam must send her away with a get, lest she became pregnant by the first husband, and she is forbidden to his brother the yavam (there, halacha 23).
perhaps you are my son and your mother is fit for levirate marriage. And if so his law is that of a yavam who inherits his deceased brother's property (as above 3:7).
and so is the law of the doubtful one with the sons of the yavam. If the yavam died before dividing the inheritance with the doubtful one, and his certain sons claim the inheritance.
they divide equally. The property of the deceased whose wife was taken in levirate marriage.
if I am your brother, give me a share in this inheritance. For his law is to receive a share in the inheritance like each of the brothers.
and if I am not your brother, return to me the half that your father took. For if he is the son of the first brother who died, he inherits him, not the yavam.
this doubtful one has no share with them in their father's estate. He does not inherit with them as one of the brothers, because of the doubt whether he is the son of the first brother.

and he cannot take it out of their hands. He cannot demand that they return the half their father took from the estate of the first brother, since judgment was already given and the doubtful heir shared with the yavam; he cannot now come and contest the division.

to divide the estate of the yavam's father. The grandfather died, and the yavam and the doubtful heir come to divide the inheritance. The yavam claims his own share and the share of his dead brother. The doubtful heir claims he is the son of the dead man and claims his share.
the yavam is a certain heir. For he is certainly the son of the deceased.
and the doubtful one is pushed aside. For wherever there is a doubtful claimant and a certain one, the doubtful one is pushed aside in favor of the certain one, as above 5:1.
and I have half. For he inherits the grandfather in place of his father.
and the two of you have half. The share of their father, the yavam, in the grandfather's estate.
and the sixth. One sixth.

the doubtful heir died, etc. The yavam and his father come to inherit him. The yavam claims that the doubtful heir was his (the dead brother's) son, while the grandfather claims that the doubtful heir was born of his son who died, and therefore he is entitled to inherit him.
the yavam died. Without other children, and the doubtful heir and the grandfather come to inherit him.
the husband's heirs. His children by another wife, or his father, or his brothers.

the wife's heirs. From her father's family, or children she had from another husband (but if they have children together, those children inherit the estate both from the husband's side and from the wife's side).

how is their case decided, etc. Since there is a doubt here, we follow the presumption of possession of the property, and give it to the heirs of whoever was in possession of it (similar to what was mentioned above in 3:9; see the explanation there).

and the ketubah, principal and addition. The obligation that the husband takes upon himself at the time of marriage to pay the wife if he dies or divorces her. It includes both the fixed sum set by the Sages (the "principal") and the addition he added of his own accord to that sum (see Hilchot Ishut 10:7).

if the house fell on him and on his mother. And it is not known who died first, so there is a doubt whether the mother's inheritance goes to her relatives or to the son's relatives (this speaks of a case where the son has no children; if he has, they inherit both from the son's side and from the mother's side).

they establish the mother's estate in the presumptive possession of the mother's heirs, who are certain heirs. The mother's relatives are certainly in the status of her heirs, and therefore are in possession of the inheritance. But the son's heirs who are not of the mother's family are not in the status of heirs by virtue of their closeness to her; they inherit her only if the son died after her (in which case they inherit her through him). Since here there is a doubt whether this is what happened, they are heirs only by doubt (Yad Peshutah).
for if the son died first, his paternal brothers have no share at all in his mother's estate. For in this case the inheritance does not pass to the family of the son's father.
as we have explained. Above 1:13.

the house fell on him and on his daughter's son. And it is not known who died first, the father or the grandson (this speaks of a case where the grandfather had only one daughter, whose son is the one who inherits the grandfather).

if the father died first, his daughter's son inherits him, and the property turns out to belong to the son's heirs. For if the grandfather died first, the grandson acquired the inheritance, and after his death his heirs, who are his father's family, receive it.

and if his daughter's son died first, the son does not inherit his mother in the grave, as we have explained. Above 1:13. Since his daughter's son died before him, the grandfather's estate, which passes to his mother, does not reach him while he is in the grave, but goes to the grandfather's heirs.

therefore the father's heirs divide with the heirs of the daughter's son. Both inherit by doubt. And although here too, as in the previous halakhah, the father's heirs are certainly in the status of heirs while the son's heirs are not in such a status, the father's heirs do not take all the property. The reason is that in the case discussed here the inheritance passed from the grandfather to his deceased daughter, and thereby left the presumptive possession of the grandfather's heirs. Since both sides have an equal doubt whether they inherit it or not, they divide (Kesef Mishneh, following the explanation of the Rosh).
and likewise, if the father was taken captive and his daughter's son died in the country. They are not in the same place, and it is not known who died first.
the house fell on him. And he had no property except what he inherits from his father.
his other bequeathers. Other relatives whom he inherits.
and we have a claim to collect from his share. For the property he inherited from his father was pledged to the debt.

the property is in the presumptive possession of the heirs. Since they inherit in any case, whether the father died before the son or after him. If the creditors want to collect their debt from them, they must bring proof that the father died first and the son inherited him.
a person cannot bequeath, etc. Specifically in the language of inheritance; but he can give as a gift, as below in halakhah 5.

even though this is monetary matter. Ordinarily in a monetary matter a person can stipulate as he wishes even against what is written in the Torah, but in inheritance a stipulation is of no effect (see also Hilchot Ishut 12:9).
for this statute. The laws of inheritance in the Torah.

whether he was critically ill. A dangerously ill person about to die. Although he can make changes in the inheritance (as explained below in halakhah 2), he cannot uproot the law of inheritance entirely.
where he has a daughter. When he has no son, in which case the daughter is the heir.

but if he had many heirs, etc. Although he cannot bequeath to one who is not fit to inherit him, a critically ill person can decide how to divide the inheritance among those who are fit to inherit him. From the verse "on the day he causes his sons to inherit" (Deuteronomy 21:16), it is learned that close to his death ("on the day he causes to inherit") a father may decide how to apportion the inheritance among his sons (see Bava Batra 130a-131a).

so-and-so my brother shall inherit me out of all my brothers. That he alone will inherit from among the brothers who are fit to inherit (when he has no children or father, and his brothers inherit him).
but if he wrote all his property to his son, he has made him only a steward. Because we estimate that he wrote so in order that all the other sons would obey this son.
as we have explained. Hilchot Zekhiyah UMatanah 6:2-3.
his words stand. As stated in the previous halakhah.
to give the firstborn's portion. To give him the firstborn's share.
and if he was healthy he cannot, etc. For the ability to decide how to apportion the inheritance is given only to a critically ill person.

in what case are these words said. That a healthy person, and likewise a critically ill person, cannot give to one who is not fit to inherit him, or reduce the firstborn's share, and likewise that a healthy person cannot change the division of the inheritance among the heirs.
if he gave a gift, his words stand. For a person may give his property as a gift, and the Torah was strict only about an inheritance that is made out of its proper order.
one who divides his property. In the language of a gift.
by his word. Orally.

when he is critically ill. Then he can do so orally, because the words of a critically ill person are considered as if written in a document and delivered into the hand of the recipient, and in this way the gift takes effect after his death (Hilchot Zekhiyah UMatanah 8:2; for the details of the laws of acquisition by a critically ill person see chapters 8-12 there). But if he is healthy, he can divide his property as a gift only by writing a will and performing a kinyan (act of acquisition), and in this way the gift takes effect during his lifetime unless he stipulated that it take effect after death (for the manner of conveying after death see 12:14-15 there).
he wrote. In a will, and likewise a critically ill person who commanded orally.
as a gift. In the language of a gift.
the time of a speech. The length of time it takes a student to say to his teacher, "Peace upon you, my teacher" (Hilchot Shevuot 2:17).
how does he say it. The language of a mixed gift to three, mentioned at the end of the previous halakhah.
by their words. By the words of the Sages (see above 1:8).

unless he stipulated with her when she was betrothed. After she was betrothed but not yet married to him. Since he is not yet entitled to inherit her (as above 1:9), he can stipulate that he will not inherit her after the marriage. For an inheritance one has not yet acquired, one can waive.
as we have explained in Hilchot Ishut. 12:9, 23:5-6.
a gentile inherits his father. And there is no difference between a son and a daughter (Rashi, Yevamot 62a).
their other inheritances we leave them according to their custom. If a gentile has no children, he is treated according to their laws.
he does not inherit his father. Since after he converted his family lineage was annulled (Hilchot Issurei Biah 14:11).
lest he return to his rebelliousness. That because of the loss of the inheritance he will return to behaving as a gentile.
that the stipulation is effective in this inheritance. And the gentile father can bequeath to another.

and a convert does not inherit a convert. Even if the son was born after his father converted, since he was conceived before his father converted, he does not inherit him (Hilchot Zekhiyah UMatanah 9:7).
gives his property to others. In the ways explained above in halakhot 5-7.
and left the heirs. Disinherited his heirs.
even though the heirs do not treat him properly. They do not treat the bequeather as they should.
and the others acquire everything he gives them. Even though the Sages do not look favorably on it, what is done is done.
who apostatized. Who converted out of his religion.
inherits his relatives. For although he apostatized, his family lineage was not annulled.
the authority is in their hands. For the court has the power to expropriate money if they see a need for it (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 24:6).
sons in Israel. Fit sons who did not apostatize.
the inheritance of their apostate father shall be given to them. The inheritance that their father was due to receive passes to them.
in the West. Spain or North Africa.
the Sages commanded. Good advice, not binding (Yad Peshutah).
clear proof. Witnesses who saw him die, or who testify to things that prove with high probability that he died, as below in halakhah 3.
they heard that he died. And there was no valid testimony about it, for example where one witness testified (Lechem Mishneh).
speaking innocently. Speaking in good faith, without intention to testify.

even though they permit his wife to remarry, etc. The Sages made it easier for a married woman to remarry on the basis of one witness or an invalid witness, so that she not remain an agunah (see Hilchot Gerushin 12:15-16, 13:29), and since she was permitted to remarry she collects her ketubah, for so it is stated explicitly in the ketubah (see Hilchot Ishut 16:31). But for the matter of inheritance, two valid witnesses are needed, as in every monetary matter.
even though she is believed. See Hilchot Gerushin 12:15.
she said, my husband died. Without children, and therefore she is to undergo yibbum (levirate marriage) (ibid.).

he shall arise upon the name of his dead brother, and he has arisen. From this the Sages learned that since he performs yibbum with his brother's wife, he is entitled to inherit him, even when there are not two valid witnesses (see Yevamot 117a).
in waters that have no end. Such as the sea, which cannot be seen in its entirety at one glance.
and his memory was lost. That they heard nothing more from him.
for we do not permit his wife to remarry at the outset. Lest he have come out from another place (Hilchot Gerushin 13:16).
into a lions' den. A pit for confining lions.
crucified. Hanged.
and died. In their opinion, but not that they saw him die.
distinctive marks on his body. Marks specific to him, such as a mole in a certain place on his body (and compare Hilchot Gerushin 13:21).

in all these cases and the like, etc. In all these cases the chance of surviving is slim, and therefore if nothing more was heard from him, his relatives inherit his property. However, since there is some chance that he was saved, we do not permit his wife to remarry, as explained shortly.

for they were strict in these matters only because of the prohibition punishable by karet. The prohibition of a married woman is among the forbidden relations punishable by karet (Hilchot Issurei Biah 1:1), and therefore they were strict to require certain testimony of the husband's death. And although they were lenient regarding a woman's testimony, that concerns the rules governing the validity of witnesses (and for the reason explained above in halakhah 1), but the testimony itself must be clear and certain (see Hilchot Gerushin 13:15). In monetary matters, by contrast, since there are two valid witnesses to the matter, one may rely on reasonable inferences.
and it was heard that he died. The rumor spread about it.
we do not take it out of their hands. Because there is a reasonable chance that he died, and they have the right to inherit.
and likewise one who fled because of danger. About whom they heard that he died.
one who left knowingly. Of his own free will.
they take it out of their hands. Since he left of his own will, we are not so concerned that he died, even though they heard that he died.
a captive who was taken captive, and a fugitive who fled because of danger to life. And their situation is not known.
the court is obligated to occupy itself with their property. To arrange for its care, in a way that will allow it to be returned properly to the owners.
trusted by the court. To guard them.
relatives who are fit to inherit. Since the relatives will care for the land better because of the chance that the land will fall to them by inheritance (Sma 285:4, and see there another reason).
until it becomes known that they died. Not by rumor but clearly (see above halakhah 1).
they assess... what they did and what they ate. They make an account of expenses and income, and give them a certain percentage of the profit, and the rest is given to the owners.
according to the custom of all the sharecroppers of that country. The percentage is set according to what is customary in that place.

and why should the court not appoint a steward forever over everything, etc. Instead of leaving the movable property in the hands of the court and the land in the hands of one fit to inherit, a steward could be appointed over the property who would manage it himself for the benefit of the owners, with full responsibility to care for it, make a profit, and return it at the end to the owners, as is done with minor heirs (see below 10:6).

because the court is not obligated to appoint a steward for adults who are of sound mind. Only for minor orphans, or a deaf-mute or an insane person (ibid. 10:8). For the property of adults no permanent steward is appointed, but its safekeeping is arranged in another way. With movable property the heir might squander it, and when the owner returns nothing would be left for him, so the court deposits it with a trustworthy person; with land, however, the heir who wants to receive its fruits will look after it more carefully, so the court need not trouble itself to look for a trustworthy person (Yad Peshutah).
standing grain. Grain.
that are like detached produce. That have ripened and can be enjoyed immediately.
and he eats them. Instead of selling them and keeping the money for the owners.
those made for rent. Which are rented out.
they do not bring down an heir for them. As with movable property, above halakhah 5.
for he collects the rent and eats. He would enjoy them and not care for them properly.
a collector. One who collects money.
until proof comes that he died. And then the rent is given to his relatives, the heirs.
fallow. Uncultivated.
and desolate. Barren.
and if he went down, they remove him. Perhaps the owner did not want him to go down.
for he left knowingly and left his property. Unattended, and this is like an object lost knowingly, as follows.
those that are in his hand. If they are in the hand of another, they remain in his hand.
one who left him as a resident. If a person left someone to live in his field.
we do not take rent from him. The heirs do not collect rent from him for his living on the land until it becomes known that the owner of the land died.
they remain as he left them until he comes. The heirs cannot end his tenancy until it becomes known that the one who left has died.
and a lost object lost knowingly, we are not commanded to return it. See also Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 11:11.
they heard that he died. The one who left knowingly.
they take out all the movable property. For if he indeed died, the heirs will not lose, unlike the law of a captive whose condition is unknown, above halakhah 5.
when they bring down the relative. As above 7:5-10.
and they do not bring down a relative to the property of a minor. Rather, they appoint a steward over his property.
this is my share that comes to me by my inheritance. For both are heirs of the same bequeather.
a relative by way of a relative. Who is not his direct heir.

for a minor cannot protest, etc. Because of his ignorance he would not know at all that this land belonged to him and fell to him by inheritance, and would not come to protest to his adult relative who holds it. But if another person who is not his relative went down, everyone knows that he is not an heir, and they will inform the minor.
the son of this minor's brother. Who inherits through his father (a relative by way of a relative).
on account of the mother's brothers. For example, the minor has a maternal brother, and that brother has a son.
who are not fit to inherit. As above 1:6.
even if there was a deed of division between them. That arranges the division among them.
whether in houses. Even if there are neighbors who live beside it and know that it was the minor's father's and that the property is his.
and he claims that this is an inherited share that came to him through him. That he inherited them directly (in the case of a relative).
or through his bequeather. That his bequeather inherited them and he inherited from him (in the case of a relative by way of a relative).
they do not bring down this remaining daughter to the property. To the property of the old woman who was taken captive, as is usually done with the property of one taken captive (above 7:5).
lest the old woman died, and a third of this property turns out to belong to the minor. For the old woman's property is divided among her three daughters, and the minor inherits his mother's share.
and likewise they do not bring down this minor to the property. That he should care for his grandmother's property until it becomes clear what happened to her.
since a steward must be appointed for the minor's half. For if both captive women died, the minor and the daughter divide the inheritance equally.
they appoint a steward over all the old woman's property. Even though ordinarily the court need not find a steward for an adult's share (above 7:5).

and the third of the captive daughter. Is in doubt, since it is not known whether she died. And since a steward is brought down for the minor's share in that third, the steward goes down also for the daughter's share in that third.
the profit is for the middle. They divide it equally, as partners do (see also Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 8:7).
they improved it for the middle. They divide the profits equally.
see what Father left us, and we are working and eating. Meaning they announce that they want to receive for themselves what they earn.
on account of themselves. For they spent expenses from the inheritance property (Maggid Mishneh).
she is the heir. Not because she is his wife, but because she is his relative.

among her sisters. Together with her sisters. For example, Reuven and Shimon are brothers; Reuven had no children, and Shimon has several daughters, and Reuven married one of Shimon's daughters. Reuven died, and after him Shimon died; it turns out that Shimon's daughters inherit their uncle, among them Reuven's wife.

among her uncles' daughters. For example, Reuven, Shimon and Levi are brothers; Reuven has one daughter, Shimon has no children, and Levi has daughters. Reuven's daughter married Shimon. Reuven and Levi died, and after them Shimon also died; it turns out that Reuven's daughter and Levi's daughters inherit Shimon.
the improvement is hers. And we do not say that she waived it because of the good name she gained by helping the orphans.
and afterward it became known that he has brothers in another country. And it became clear that he is a partner with his brothers in the inherited property.
he improved it for the middle. As above in halakhah 2.

since he did not know... we assess for him as a sharecropper. For it is possible that had he known he had brothers, he would not have been willing to labor for them. And since the brothers are not here, the property has the law of a captive's property, where a relative is brought down to the land to work it and takes a sharecropper's wage (above 7:5; but with minors we do not say so, because a relative is not brought down to a minor's property - Bava Metzia 39b-40a).

and likewise a brother who went down to the property of a minor and improved it. He knew he had a minor brother and went down to his property, although the court does not bring down a relative to a minor's property (above 8:1).
who took money. From the inheritance, before they divided it among themselves.

who does not leave his Torah. But only for his livelihood, and this is as if he had stipulated explicitly and said, "See what Father left us..." (Rabbi Yosef Migash, Shapira edition, Bava Batra 143b).

one of the brothers. Who are partners in the inheritance and have not yet divided it (compare Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 8:7, and see Chasdei David, Bava Batra 10:2, who discusses the relation between the two halakhot).
a collector. One appointed to collect various taxes and debts.
a scribe. One responsible for recording income.
known for this matter. Skilled in this work.
the extra payment. Payment beyond what is due him for his work.
the wage. The compensation for the work.
conducts business within the household. Engages in commerce for the family.
in his name alone. That the documents were written in his name alone.
from my mother's father's house. And his brothers were born of another mother, and therefore he inherited the money alone (see above 1:6).
he must bring proof. Lest he took from the inheritance money and used it for his own needs.

and likewise the woman who conducts business within the household. A married woman who deals with her husband's property (compare Hilchot Ishut 22:30, which speaks of when she does not conduct business - Kesef Mishneh there).
they fell to me by inheritance. From her father's family.
nedunya. The property she brought with her into the marriage from her father's house, which returns fully to her ownership after her husband's death (see Hilchot Ishut 16:1).
and she said, I bought it from my nedunya, she is believed. Since it is known that she has money of her own, it can be attributed to that.
for they do not divide their dough. They are partners in all the property, even in their food.
he saved. He economized from his own, and so bought or lent.

if he died... the brothers must bring proof. Although if their father were alive he would have had to bring proof that the property is his alone (as above halakhah 7), when he has died we do not demand that the orphans bring proof, since they do not know their father's proofs.

one of the brothers from whose possession a promissory note emerges. Who holds a promissory note of his father in which his father lent money to another, and claims that his father gave it to him as a gift.

by writing and delivery. A promissory note is not acquired like other movable property, until the giver writes to the recipient that he transfers to him the note and its lien, and in addition delivers the note into his hand (Hilchot Mekhirah 6:11).
or he commanded it to him when he was critically ill. In the case of a critically ill person, the Sages enacted that he can transfer a promissory note by speech (see Hilchot Zekhiyah UMatanah 10:2).
in what case are these words said. That one who holds a promissory note in which another borrowed must bring proof.
they snatch from one another. They rule that it is permitted to snatch from one another, because all are heirs.
that was given to him. As a gift.
he collects with it and need not bring proof. See Hilchot Mekhirah 6:11, Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 16:7.
one of the brothers who took. From the joint inheritance, before they divided it among themselves, and went to another place.
the household's blessing. The proportional share in the joint food expenses.
for the expense of food, etc. For the expense of food diminishes proportionally as the number of household members grows (see also Hilchot Ishut 18:4).

the adults are not supported, etc. Naturally, adults' expenses for clothing are greater than the minors', and the minors' expense for food is greater than the adults'. As long as they have not divided the inheritance money among themselves, we do not say that each takes his needs from the joint property and divides what remains, but they are given their expenses equally and each is supported from his own share (Arukh HaShulchan 286:1).
the adults married. They got married, and took the wedding expenses from the joint property.
the minors also take from the estate. The same amount that the adults spent.
the adults married in their father's lifetime. And their father gave them from his own.
we are marrying as you married. They want to take the wedding expenses from the joint property just as the brothers who married in the father's lifetime received.

we do not listen to them. All this is regarding sons. But regarding daughters, the Sages enacted that if he married off one daughter in his lifetime and left another daughter who was unmarried, the second takes for her marriage as the elder took (Hilchot Ishut 20:3).

and a shoshvinut was sent to this son in his father's lifetime. In their days it was the custom that when a person married, his friends sent him gifts for the expenses of the feast, and came and rejoiced with him. These gifts are called shoshvinut. The shoshvinut is not a full gift but a kind of loan, since the person sends it on the understanding that his friend the groom will return it when he marries (Hilchot Zekhiyah UMatanah 7:1-2). In the case discussed here, the wedding feast expenses were the groom's father's, and therefore the shoshvinut is considered a loan given to the father.
when it is returned. To the friend who sent the shoshvinut, when he marries.

it is returned from the middle. Since the feast expenses came from the father, the father became obligated to return the shoshvinut he received, and when he died the inheritance property became obligated.

but if the son spent on the feast from his own, etc. When the wedding feast expenses were the son's, the shoshvinut is a debt that rests on him alone, and therefore it is returned from his share of the inheritance and not from the general property of the inheritance.
shoshvinut in the name of one of his sons. That the father specified that the gift is sent in the name of one of the sons.
it is his. Alone.

and the one to whom it was sent is not obligated to return it until all the sons rejoice with him, etc. The obligation to return the entire shoshvinut applies only when the giver marries and invites the recipient of the shoshvinut to rejoice and dine with him at his wedding feast (Hilchot Zekhiyah UMatanah 7:3 and halakhah 9 there). Since the shoshvinut was given in the name of all the sons, all the sons must invite him to rejoice at their weddings, and he returns to each one a proportional share of the total sum.

if he rejoiced with some of them, he returns only the part of the one with whom he rejoiced. For example, if there were three sons and he rejoiced with one of them, he returns a third of the shoshvinut.
and it is for the middle. All will benefit from that part that was returned, as with a debt the debtor paid to their father.
his words are heard. In conducting business for the brothers, because he appears distinguished.
from the household's holdings. The joint property before the heirs divided it.
and a brother came to them. Whom they did not know about, and they divided the inheritance without him.
a creditor. Who lent money to their father.

even if this one took land and this one money. A creditor collecting from the heirs collects only from land (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 11:7). And when one took money and one took land, we do not say that he took land on the understanding that if a creditor comes he will collect from him; rather the division is void.
the division is void. The division of the property, and each of the brothers can demand to redivide the property.
and they go back and divide the rest. What remains after the lender has collected his debt.
at the time of his illness. When he was critically ill, whose words are as if written and delivered (Hilchot Zekhiyah UMatanah 8:2).
the brothers who divided. Who come to divide, after having at first used the property jointly and bought clothes for themselves and their families with it.
they assess what is on them. They estimate the value of the clothes they bought from the joint property, and deduct it from the inheritance.

for they already acquired them for themselves. The children and wives acquire the clothes bought for them, and they do not belong to the joint inheritance money (see also Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 1:5, Hilchot Arakhin VeCharamin 3:14).
but for Shabbat and festival clothes, etc. Which are more expensive and not a basic need, the brothers do not transfer ownership of them to their sons and wives.
a steward. An agent or trustee who has the right to manage the property and affairs of another.
and he chooses for them the better portion. They select for each one a portion that is fitting and suitable for him.
they cannot protest. And demand another portion, claiming that they have preference in another portion.
the court erred in the valuation and reduced it by a sixth. They valued the minors' property at a sixth less than its true worth.

they can protest. Ordinarily when there is an error of a sixth ("shetut") the sale stands and the difference must be returned, and when the error is more than a sixth the sale is void (Hilchot Mekhirah 12:2). But when a court errs the law is different, and even with an error of a sixth the sale can be cancelled (ibid. 13:10; and for the law of a steward who erred see halakhah 9 there).
after they grew up. And the orphans discovered the error.
he must appoint. Before his death.
occupies himself. Tends to.
the father of orphans. They are charged with the welfare of the orphans.
the authority is in his hand. For a person may deal with his property as he wishes, and the court need not appoint a steward.
if he appointed... a minor or a woman or a slave. To occupy themselves with the property of his minor heirs.
not a woman. For it is not a woman's way to go out and come in and toil with property (Rashi, Gittin 52a).
and not a slave. A Canaanite slave, who is not trustworthy (ibid.).
an am ha'aretz who is presumed suspect of transgressions. See Hilchot Edut 11:1-2.
and a man of valor. Who does not fear to save the orphans' property (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 2:7).
strength in the affairs of the world. Who knows how to conduct business.
a relative shall not go down to the land. For we do not bring down a relative to the property of an heir, as above 8:1.
more than an amount he is estimated to have. More than what, according to the assessment of his property, it can be assumed he spent from his own.
perhaps he found a lost article. And the expenses he spent came from the profit he gained from that found article.
they remove him. For had the father known of this, he would not have appointed him.
that we make him swear since he caused a loss. Although ordinarily we do not make a steward appointed by the father swear (compare below 11:5).
his reputation is good. That he is known as a fit person.
who was lax with vows. Who makes many vows, and it can be assumed that he does not always keep his word (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 2:3).
and with the dust of robbery. Acts of transgression akin to robbery, such as dice playing (see Hilchot Edut 10:4).
for every court is the father of orphans. For the court in every place and time must see to the welfare of orphans.
and we do not appoint a steward for him. Since he is of sound mind he must look after himself, and the court is not obligated to do so (above 7:5).
unless his father or his bequeather commanded that they not give him, etc. See Piskei VeShitot.
and they appoint a steward for them. See also Hilchot Mekhirah 29:4.
orphans' money... does not need a steward. Unlike other property, for which the court appoints a steward to tend to it (see above 10:5 and below halakhah 4).

they investigate who has property that has security and is of the best quality. They look for a person who has excellent land. Such a person's financial situation is stable and investing with him carries no great risk.
he did not accept excommunication upon himself. That the court had not placed him under a ban.

close to profit and far from loss. In a way that the orphans are very likely to profit and not lose. They agree with him that if there is a profit on the money the orphans receive it, and if there is a loss he pays it to them from his own pocket. Although a loan on these terms is forbidden by rabbinic law as a hint of interest, with orphans' property they did not forbid it (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 4:14).
a pledge. To secure the orphans' money.
broken gold. Pieces of gold not made into objects and jewelry.
that has no identifying mark. And therefore there is no concern that others will come and claim it by means of identifying marks.
jewelry. An ornament.

and they give an identifying mark and take it after his death if the judge knows that this is not estimated. If a person comes and claims that he deposited an object with the deceased before his death, and gives identifying marks, the object is taken from the orphans and given to him, provided that the judge knows the deceased and knows that, according to the estimate of his wealth, it is not plausible that the object was his (see Hilchot Sheelah UFikadon 6:4).
and how much shall they set for the profit. What percentage of the profits the one who engages in business receives.
with the money. The surplus beyond their food needs.
and they shall hand it over to the steward. As above 10:5.
and they sell them immediately. Lest they be stolen or spoil (Meiri, Ketubot 100b).
and if the market is near the town they take them to the market. For their price there is higher, but if it was far they do not take them, lest they be lost on the way.
and their proceeds are combined with the money. And they treat them as they treat money, as above halakhah 1.
shekhar. An intoxicating drink made from fruit or grain.
according to the property. According to the assets they have.
and according to what is fitting for them. According to their needs and their station.
and he shall not give them too much luxury. He should not provide for their needs lavishly and in excess.
gives them. The steward.

and he swears, by taking hold of an object, that he did not rob them of anything. Since he might permit himself to take the heirs' money because of the trouble he takes for them, the Sages enacted that he can be required to swear on a doubtful claim when there is suspicion that he took money, even if there is no certainty about it (Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 9:1, where other cases of those who swear on a doubtful claim for similar reasons are mentioned; and see there later in the chapter various laws relating to this oath). This oath is taken by holding an object, namely while holding a Torah scroll in his hand (Hilchot Shevuot 11:8).

when the court appointed him. People want the court to appoint them as stewards so that their trustworthiness will become known among people, and they are not deterred by being obligated to swear (Commentary on the Mishnah, Gittin 5:4; and see also Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 9:4).
but a steward appointed by the orphans' father, etc. If the orphans' father or another person who bequeathed the property appointed the steward.
does not swear on a doubtful claim. Since the steward receives no payment for his work, they exempted him from an oath on a doubtful claim so that he would not refrain from being a steward.
the steward may. He is permitted.
so that he will be honored. As with an elder brother, above 9:15.
stewards may sell, etc. But they may not give a gift (Hilchot Mekhirah 30:6).
to feed the orphans. For their sustenance.
but they do not sell and leave the money. Lest it be stolen, or because the property is more valuable (Rashi, Gittin 52a).
and they do not sell fields to buy slaves. In order to buy slaves.
the main part of all field property. Which serves for working the field, and without oxen the field work cannot be carried out.
to sell far and redeem near. To sell fields located far away in order to buy fields closer by.

to litigate and incur liability in order to win. To represent the orphans in a lawsuit and obligate them in some matter, even though they think this may result in a greater gain for the orphans from another direction (Merkevet HaMishneh; see Maggid Mishneh, who explained it differently).
stewards are not permitted to free slaves. For they may only sell in order to feed the orphans.
and even to take from the slave, etc. Because it looks like freeing without payment, and from this people would come to treat orphans' property lightly (Tosafot, Gittin 38b).
they sell. The slave, for the orphans' support.
on condition that they free him. That is, the buyers have permission to free him if they wish (Perishah; and compare Hilchot Arakhin VeCharamin 6:18).
they separate terumah. And they should not separate with a generous eye, but one sixtieth of the produce (Hilchot Terumot 3:3).

but they sell it as tevel. And they do not first separate terumah and tithes from it. Although ordinarily it is forbidden to sell tevel, the Sages permitted it when there is a need, such as in this case, which is done for the benefit of orphans (see Hilchot Maaser 6:6).
a fixed sum. A price known in advance.
who are not obligated in any of the commandments. For a minor under the age of thirteen is not obligated in the commandments by Torah law.
in order to educate them. To train them in the commandments (for further examples see Hilchot Tefillin 4:13, Hilchot Tzitzit 3:9, Hilchot Berakhot 5:1).
we do not set a charity pledge on them. But in order to give them standing, it is permitted to set one on them (Hilchot Matanot Aniyim 7:12).
and even for the redemption of captives. Which is an exceedingly important commandment (ibid. 8:10).
they set one on him. Since charity is an obligation upon him, his property is bound for it (Kesef Mishneh).
if he was fit. According to his financial situation.
as we have explained. Above halakhah 5.

and be very careful of the Father of these orphans, who rides the heavens. A name for the Holy One, blessed be He, who rules the highest firmament, in which are righteousness and just judgment, in which life, peace and blessing are stored, to bestow good on those who do righteousness, justice and charity (Arukh HaShulchan 290:34).
extol. Praise and exalt.
